title: Indian Truck Simulator Rebuilds Delhi's Real Road Network for a 2027 PC Release
excerpt: IronFort Studios' single-player trucking game is built from real Delhi-NCR map data — NH44 to the Delhi-Meerut Expressway — with painted trucks, dhaba stops, fatigue that builds faster in afternoon heat, and a Steam wishlist open now.
body:
• Indian Truck Simulator, from indie developer IronFort Studios, is slated for a 2027 release and is available to wishlist on Steam now.
  • Every road is built from real map data of Delhi-NCR, across Delhi, Haryana and western Uttar Pradesh, with interchanges rebuilt at true scale and longer highway sections shortened so a haul fits into an evening.
  • Gameplay is the work of trucking: pick loads by pay per km, weight or deadline — grain sacks, LPG cylinders, crates — and manage diesel, damage, fatigue and late-delivery penalties.
  • It is single-player, needs no internet and has no ads or energy timers; buses, autos, tractors and two-wheelers in traffic, truck decoration, and steering wheel and gamepad support are listed as coming before release.

A new trucking game is being built around the roads its players actually know. Indian Truck Simulator, from indie developer IronFort Studios, replicates the road network around New Delhi using real National Capital Region map data, and is slated for a 2027 release, according to Traxion. It follows the path of SCS Software's popular trucking games, tasking players with completing deliveries on time with cargo including grain sacks, LPG canisters and wooden crates.

Real roads, real distances

According to the game's Steam page, every road is built from real map data of Delhi-NCR, from NH44 to the Delhi-Meerut Expressway and the old highways beside them. Direction boards in Hindi and English give real distances to real places, and the GPS guides players along the real network lane by lane. The truck itself is a classic cowl truck covered in truck art — the ALL INDIA PERMIT board, Hindi slogans and HORN OK PLEASE across the tailgate — with working gauges, air brakes, wipers and mirrors, a shrine on the dash and a berth behind the seats.

The rhythm of the road

The simulation leans into the life around the driving. Fatigue builds as you drive, faster in the afternoon heat and the small hours; players stop at a dhaba for chai, a charpai for an hour or a room for the night, and the clock keeps running. Traffic honks to pass, flashes high beams and swings through gaps in the median, signals switch to flashing amber after eleven at night, and speed breakers wait outside villages and schools. Loads are picked from a job board by pay per km, weight or deadline; arrive late and the pay is halved, and diesel, repairs and chai all come out of the player's balance.

What to know if you want to play it

The game is single-player, needs no internet, and has no ads and no energy timers. IronFort says buses, autos, tractors and two-wheelers in traffic, truck decoration, and steering wheel and gamepad support are coming before release, and wishlisters will hear when the demo is ready. The Steam page lists a 30 GB install and, for Windows, a minimum Intel Core i5-9600K or AMD Ryzen 5 3600 with 16 GB RAM — requirements the studio notes may change before release, since the game is still in development.
